You’re probably thinking of **[`cargo-dist`](https://github.com/axodotdev/cargo-dist)**, created by **axo** around 2022–2023. It generates release CI, cross-platform binaries, installers, checksums, and GitHub Releases for Rust CLIs.

I’m checking its original feature set against its current status—the project evolved beyond its early Rust-only form, so the name and scope have shifted a bit.

The modern equivalent is actually **the same project**: `cargo-dist` was renamed **`dist`** as it expanded beyond Rust. The crate/repository still uses the `cargo-dist` name in places, but the command is now generally `dist`. It remains actively maintained; the current docs show version 0.32.0. ([repository](https://github.com/axodotdev/cargo-dist), [docs](https://axodotdev.github.io/cargo-dist/))

It automated most of the work after deciding to release:

- Read Cargo workspace/package metadata.
- Interpret release tags such as `v1.2.3` or package-specific tags.
- Generate a GitHub Actions release workflow.
- Build binaries across Linux, macOS, and Windows, including x86-64 and ARM targets.
- Package binaries into `.tar.gz`, `.tar.xz`, or `.zip` archives.
- Generate source archives and checksums.
- Create shell and PowerShell installers that detect the user’s platform.
- Generate Homebrew formulas, npm binary packages, and Windows MSI installers.
- Create the GitHub Release, assemble release notes, and upload every artifact.
- Produce a machine-readable `dist-manifest.json`.
- Optionally generate artifact attestations, updater support, and custom publishing jobs.

Its key trick was that `dist init` generated and maintained the complicated CI workflow for you. Afterward, pushing a release tag could produce a complete multi-platform GitHub Release. The supported options are documented in its [configuration reference](https://axodotdev.github.io/cargo-dist/book/reference/config.html).

One important boundary: `cargo-dist` originally concentrated on **building and distributing binaries**, not deciding the next version or preparing a release PR. A common modern stack is:

- **[`release-plz`](https://github.com/release-plz/release-plz)** — version bumps, changelogs, release PRs, tags, and crates.io publishing.
- **[`dist`](https://github.com/axodotdev/cargo-dist)** — compiled binaries, archives, installers, package-manager artifacts, and GitHub Releases.
- **[`cargo-binstall`](https://github.com/cargo-bins/cargo-binstall)** — consumer-side installation of available prebuilt binaries.

So if you were starting a Rust CLI today, `release-plz + dist` would be the fairly complete modern version of that idea.

The current mise workflow already delays expensive builds until auto-merge is armed, but a tag still starts the build matrix again. It also skips notarization during the candidate run, leaving a possible failure until publication time. The bigger improvement is to make a frozen release candidate—with retained, tested artifacts—the unit that moves through the system.

Your stats page already has much of the public dashboard vocabulary: adoption, growth rates, milestones, rankings, and forecasts. That pairs well with a private view showing release readiness, cost, and which distribution channels have caught up.

I think there’s a useful product here: **a dashboard that takes a CLI from “ready to release” through “available everywhere,” then shows how adoption changes afterward.**

The central idea should be **build a release candidate once, then promote those exact artifacts**.

Your current mise workflow already gates expensive builds on auto-merge being enabled, but tags start the build matrix again. Candidate runs also skip notarization, so they don’t exercise everything required for publication. That explains why merely rearranging the merge step won’t fully solve this.

### The release model

I’d make `workflow_dispatch` create a frozen candidate:

| Stage | What happens |
|---|---|
| Prepare | Pin a source commit, choose the final version, generate changelog/version/docs changes on a candidate branch, and open a release PR. |
| Validate | Run inexpensive checks first, then build the release binaries and packages. |
| Stage | Sign, notarize, generate installers and manifests, and retain artifacts with checksums. Test installation using those artifacts. |
| Ready | Show the candidate’s exact changes, test results, artifacts, cost, and publication plan. |
| Promote | Verify the candidate is still eligible, merge according to repository policy, create the tag, and publish the retained artifacts. |
| Verify | Check that users can actually install the release through each supported channel. |

The release PR becomes a review surface for a particular candidate. Ordinary pushes to `main` shouldn’t continually rewrite it and restart expensive builds.

**There’s one important policy choice:** what happens if `main` advances while the candidate builds?

My preference would be to let a release represent a pinned snapshot, with later commits going into the next release. Tag the tested candidate commit and reconcile its release changes into `main`. If you require the tag to identify the exact squash-merged commit instead, the system must account for changed source or build metadata; it cannot blindly reuse artifacts from the PR head.

That choice should be explicit in the product. “Always release the latest `main`” and “never rebuild a completed candidate” cannot both be guaranteed while development continues.

### Put irreversible actions at the end

Before publication, do everything that can reasonably fail:

- Validate versions, package metadata, changelogs, credentials, and destination configuration.
- Build and test the packaged binaries, including installation, PATH setup, and upgrades.
- Complete signing and notarization.
- Prepare crates and run package verification.
- Generate Homebrew/npm/MSI artifacts, checksums, attestations, and packslips.
- Confirm the candidate and its artifact inventory haven’t changed.

Cargo’s dry run verifies packaging, but the registry still performs additional checks when publishing. Some failures therefore remain possible after promotion begins. ([Cargo publishing documentation](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/publishing.html))

So the system needs a **persistent publication journal**. If crates.io succeeds and npm fails, the dashboard should say precisely that and offer “retry npm.” It should retain successful artifacts and resume incomplete steps, checking the destination before retrying an ambiguous upload.

There is no atomic transaction across GitHub, crates.io, npm, and Homebrew. Making partial publication understandable and recoverable is a substantial part of the product.

### What the dashboard could do

I’d have two views sharing the same project and release data.

**Private maintainer view**

- All projects: ready candidates, failed releases, unpublished changes, and channels awaiting updates.
- Release details: source commit, version, changes, target matrix, artifact digests, and test evidence.
- Actions: prepare, promote, supersede, retry a failed step.
- CI accounting: time and estimated cost per release, expensive targets, retries, and duplicated work.
- Distribution status: “GitHub available; crates.io available; Homebrew PR awaiting merge.”
- Scheduled releases with rules such as your weekly cadence and pending `fix`/`feat` requirement.

**Public project view**

Your [mise-analytics](https://github.com/jdx/mise-analytics) and [mise versions stats](https://mise-versions.jdx.dev/stats) already supply a strong starting point:

- Downloads, stars, Homebrew installs/rank, growth, and milestones.
- Release timelines overlaid on those charts.
- Platform-specific downloads and installation instructions.
- Public channel freshness and supported-platform status.
- Shareable milestone cards and embeddable badges.
- Version adoption where there is an appropriate data source.

Keep metric definitions visible. Downloads, stars, package-manager installs, and estimated active users measure different things; they shouldn’t become one combined “users” count. Forecasts should also show their assumptions.

### Other features I’d prioritize

The most valuable additions connect release quality to distribution:

1. **Installability checks.** Regularly install the latest version on clean machines and report broken URLs, installers, signatures, or platform compatibility.
2. **Release comparisons.** Binary size, startup performance, minimum OS/glibc requirements, dependency changes, and CLI compatibility.
3. **Channel propagation tracking.** Measure how long each ecosystem takes to receive a release and detect channels that silently stop updating.
4. **Recovery controls.** Deprecate a bad release, move a mutable stable channel back where supported, and guide the maintainer through publishing a fix.
5. **Shared organization policies.** Configure signing, targets, release cadence, and publishing conventions once across your CLIs, with project overrides.

I’d build this as an open-source CLI and release-state format, a reusable GitHub workflow, and a dashboard/GitHub App. Builds can stay on the user’s existing runners. Existing `dist` setups and custom build commands should both plug in; packslip could supply the signed artifact inventory.

For the first version, I’d prove it with one simpler CLI and then mise: **dispatch → frozen candidate → build/test/stage → promote without rebuilding → resumable publication**. Pair that with a public stats page using your existing collectors. That establishes the two strongest reasons to use it: cheaper, more dependable releases and a useful public home for the project’s growth.

Yes—**release lines** should be a first-class concept. Each project could have multiple lines, each with its own source branch, version policy, channel, and release candidates.

For example:

| Release line | Branch | Versions | Distribution |
|---|---|---|---|
| Stable | `main` | `1.8.0`, `1.8.1` | Default installation |
| Next major | `next` or `v2` | `2.0.0-alpha.1`, `2.0.0-beta.1`, `2.0.0-rc.1` | Opt-in prereleases |
| Maintenance | `v1` | `1.8.2`, `1.8.3` | Supported older major |

Branch names should be configurable. The product tracks what the branch *means*, rather than requiring a particular naming convention.

A **“Start next major”** action could create the branch and configure its prerelease sequence, leaving stable releases operating independently. The dashboard would show what’s breaking, which fixes haven’t reached both lines, and what remains before v2 is ready.

Some particularly useful behavior:

- **Semver guidance:** suggest a bump from commit intent and compatibility checks, with maintainer override. For CLIs, compatibility includes flags, configuration, environment variables, machine-readable output, and exit codes—not just Rust APIs.
- **Backport tracking:** mark a fix as needed on v1, v2, or both; offer a cherry-pick PR and track completion.
- **Prerelease channels:** give testers a consistent way to install the newest alpha/beta/RC without changing what normal users receive.
- **Major-release readiness:** collect migration notes, removed deprecations, compatibility checks, and outstanding blockers.
- **Graduation:** release v2 as stable, update default installation channels, and optionally keep v1 as a maintenance line.
- **Support policy:** show which majors receive fixes and when their support ends.

One subtlety with our “build once” model: **promoting an RC to stable generally requires a new build**, because `2.0.0-rc.3` and `2.0.0` are different versions embedded in binaries and packages. We should promise that the final `2.0.0` candidate is built and tested once before publication, rather than promise to relabel an RC’s bytes.

That gives the dashboard a useful hierarchy: **project → release line → candidate → artifacts and publication status**. It would handle both your current frequent releases and a deliberate, months-long v2 development cycle.

content.text:
**D1 would hold Envol’s coordination state; R2 would hold the files we’ve built and intend to publish.** GitHub would still hold the source, PRs, and workflow logs.

| Storage | Contents |
|---|---|
| D1 | Projects, release lines, candidates, source commits, workflow run IDs, test outcomes, artifact checksums, publication progress, and daily popularity measurements |
| R2 | Candidate binaries, archives, installers, prepared packages, signatures, and manifests |

The publication journal is especially important: “crates.io succeeded; GitHub succeeded; npm needs retry” must survive a failed workflow or server restart.

R2 also lets a candidate remain releasable independently of GitHub Actions artifact retention. We could start with Actions artifacts and add R2 later, but I’d use R2 from the beginning for completed candidates. It’s artifact retention, not a compiler cache. Build and publishing credentials would stay in GitHub’s secrets/environments.

For merging back, suppose `main` is at commit **A** when you start a release:

1. Envol branches from A and commits the version/changelog changes as **R**.
2. It builds and tests R. Meanwhile, normal development moves `main` to **B**.
3. When you promote, Envol tags **R** and publishes its tested artifacts.
4. A PR merges the release branch back into `main`, preserving B’s newer changes.

With a normal merge commit, Git brings in the release changes relative to their shared ancestor A. It doesn’t replace `main` with the older snapshot. The release tag stays on R, accurately identifying the shipped source.

**The awkward cases are version files, lockfiles, and changelogs edited on both branches.** I’d make Envol check that integration before any publishing. Straightforward merges can be prepared automatically; conflicts need resolution before promotion. That resolution must not silently change the source being released.

There are two distinct choices here:

- **Merge before publication:** validate and merge the release changes, then publish R’s artifacts. A registry failure can still leave `main` bumped, but all builds, tests, signing, and notarization have already succeeded.
- **Merge after publication:** publish R, then merge the prepared PR. This keeps `main` untouched until publication succeeds, but leaves a possible integration problem afterward.

**I recommend merging before publication, after the candidate is fully validated.** Your original concern was changing `main` before knowing whether the release builds and works; this moves that change past those checks while avoiding post-publication merge trouble. We still tag R rather than the newer merge commit.

Does that tradeoff fit what you want, or is keeping `main` untouched until publishing succeeds a firm requirement?

I’d make the core portable:

| Component | Self-hosted default | Hosted deployment |
|---|---|---|

ok but what happens if commits hit main in the midst

They stay on `main` and go into the next release. The candidate stays frozen.

Suppose Envol starts from commit **A**, adds the version/changelog commit **R**, and builds R. Meanwhile, developers add **B** and **C** to `main`.

When the candidate passes:

- Envol merges R’s release changes into `main`, preserving B and C.
- It tags **R**, the exact commit it built and tested.
- It publishes R’s artifacts. B and C aren’t included in that release.

The consequence is that **the release tag is on the candidate branch’s history, not the newest commit on `main`**. With a normal merge, that tagged commit becomes an ancestor of `main`.

If the merge conflicts, promotion pauses **before tagging or publishing**. Resolving the integration PR doesn’t change R or its artifacts. If you want those resolutions—or B and C—in the release itself, Envol creates a new candidate and rebuilds.

If you want tags strictly on `main`’s first-parent history instead, we’d need either a temporary merge freeze or to invalidate the candidate whenever `main` advances. My preference is the frozen snapshot: development continues, and the tag still identifies precisely what shipped.

Yes—that simplifies the model. **Freeze `main` for the release window**, so the tested candidate can become the exact commit we tag on `main`.

The flow becomes:

1. Acquire a release lock and enforce the freeze on GitHub.
2. Prepare the version/changelog candidate from the frozen `main`.
3. Build, test, package, sign, and notarize it.
4. Advance `main` to that exact candidate commit, then create the tag.
5. Publish the retained artifacts.

If validation fails, `main` remains unchanged and Envol unlocks it. Once tagging has happened, a publishing failure becomes a resumable release; we can unlock `main` because the release is already pinned.

Yes. GitHub supports this through a **branch ruleset with “Restrict updates.”** Only actors on its bypass list can update the targeted branch, and that list can include the Envol GitHub App. This is available for public repositories on GitHub Free. ([GitHub docs](https://docs.github.com/en/repositories/configuring-branches-and-merges-in-your-repository/managing-rulesets/creating-rulesets-for-a-repository))

Envol would manage a dedicated `envol-release-freeze` ruleset targeting `main`:

1. Activate it with only Envol allowed to bypass.
2. Read `main` **after** activating the freeze, then prepare and build the candidate.
3. Advance `main` to the tested commit and create the tag.
4. Disable the freeze.

During that window, ordinary merges and direct pushes are blocked. Your existing protection rules remain in force; bypassing the freeze doesn’t automatically bypass other rulesets. ([Ruleset behavior](https://docs.github.com/en/repositories/configuring-branches-and-merges-in-your-repository/managing-rulesets/about-rulesets))

Two implementation details matter:

- **Permissions:** Envol needs repository Administration write access to toggle the ruleset, plus Contents write access to advance the branch and create tags. ([Rules API](https://docs.github.com/en/rest/repos/rules))
- **Recovery:** Envol needs cancellation cleanup and an independent recovery check so a crashed workflow doesn’t leave `main` frozen. An administrator can also disable the dedicated ruleset manually.

And a correction to my earlier wording: a normal squash merge creates a different commit. To preserve the exact SHA we tested, Envol would **fast-forward `main` to the candidate**, with an explicitly configured exception to any PR-only protection. The release PR can still provide review and checks.

So yes, it’s feasible—but installation needs to configure these permissions and protections explicitly.
and we can modify that via the api?

Yes—the [GitHub REST API](https://docs.github.com/en/rest/repos/rules#update-a-repository-ruleset) lets Envol toggle it:

```http
PUT /repos/{owner}/{repo}/rulesets/{ruleset_id}
```

Set `"enforcement": "active"` to freeze or `"enforcement": "disabled"` to unfreeze, preserving the ruleset’s other settings.

A GitHub App installation token with **Administration: write** can do this. Envol would create the dedicated ruleset during setup and toggle it for each release.

# Envol: release once, distribute reliably, track adoption

## Summary

Create **`jdx/envol`**, a public, open-source project for managing CLI releases and presenting their adoption statistics. Build a Rust CLI and portable server with a bundled web dashboard. GitHub Actions performs builds on each project’s own runners.

The first usable version will release Envol itself through the complete workflow, support stable and next-major release lines, and provide public statistics pages. Then onboard a simpler jdx CLI before migrating mise’s more expensive release pipeline.

## Product and architecture

- Use a Rust workspace for the release engine, CLI, and HTTP server; use Axum, SQLite migrations, and a TypeScript/React dashboard bundled into the server.
- Make self-hosting one container with one persistent volume. Store coordination state and metrics in SQLite, and artifacts in a local directory by default. Offer S3-compatible storage, including R2. Do not require Cloudflare, D1, or an external queue.
- Provide a GitHub App installation flow, signed webhook processing, GitHub login, and repository-scoped authorization. Keep public project pages separate from authenticated release controls.
- Run builds and publishing in reusable GitHub Actions workflows. Keep package-registry and signing credentials in the project’s GitHub secrets/environments.
- Authenticate workflow callbacks using GitHub Actions OIDC, validating repository, workflow identity, run, and candidate association.
- Support project-provided build, test, package, signing, and publishing commands. Existing custom scripts and `dist` can integrate without replacing the release engine.
- Require the server for the first complete orchestration workflow. Defer a fully independent, serverless CLI mode to avoid implementing two coordination systems initially.

## Release workflow and GitHub integration

### Candidate preparation and validation

1. Accept a release request from the dashboard, CLI, or `workflow_dispatch`, specifying the project, release line, and optional version override.
2. Acquire a persistent lock for that release line. Activate a dedicated GitHub branch ruleset restricting updates and deletions, with only the Envol App allowed to bypass.
3. Verify the ruleset is active, then read the source branch SHA. Create a candidate branch with the final version, changelog, and configured generated-file changes. Open a ready-for-review PR against the release line’s source branch.

+# Envol
+
+A release control plane for CLIs: prepare a candidate, build and test it once,
+then promote the exact tested commit and publish the retained artifacts.
+
+**Early implementation, not yet validated for production releases.** Live
+release operations are disabled unless `ENVOL_RELEASES_ENABLED=true` is set.
+
+## Architecture
+
+- Shared TypeScript API and release engine with a React dashboard.
+- Cloudflare Workers, D1, and R2 for the hosted deployment.
+- Node.js 24, SQLite, and local artifact storage for self-hosting.
+- Rust CLI in `crates/envol` for configuring and operating releases.
+- GitHub Actions runners build candidates; GitHub OIDC authenticates artifact uploads.
+
+The intended release sequence freezes the source branch with a dedicated GitHub
+ruleset, prepares an immutable candidate commit and PR, runs checks and uploads
+artifacts, fast-forwards the source branch to the tested commit, creates the tag,
+unfreezes the branch, and publishes retained artifacts. Publication is resumable.
+Release lines configure stable, next-major prerelease, and maintenance branches.
+
+## Local development
+
+```sh
+npm ci
+npm run build
+npm start
+```
+
+The dashboard listens on `http://localhost:8787`. Set `ENVOL_ADMIN_TOKEN` to enable
+administrative API access; see `.env.example` for other environment variables.
+The Node process reads environment variables supplied by the caller, so export
+them before starting. Docker Compose is also provided for SQLite self-hosting.
+
+```sh
+npm run format:check
+npm run check
+npm test
+npm run build
+npx wrangler deploy --dry-run
+cargo fmt --check
+cargo clippy --locked --all-targets -- -D warnings
+cargo test --locked
+cargo run --locked -- check
+```
+
+Database contract tests run against both Node SQLite and Miniflare D1. The CI
+`final` job requires every formatting, application, and CLI job to succeed;
+failed or unexpectedly skipped jobs cannot produce a successful gate.
+
+## Hosted deployment
+
+After merge, GitHub Actions deploys to Cloudflare using the repository secret
+`CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN`. The workflow creates Envol's D1 database and R2 bucket if
+missing, applies migrations, seeds public project trackers, and deploys the
+Worker. Configure the account and resource names in `wrangler.jsonc` for your
+own account. Initial custom-domain setup is separate; CI does not need DNS access.
+
+## Current limits
+
+- GitHub release publication is implemented; crates.io and other registry
+  publishers are not yet implemented.
+- Administration currently uses a shared token, not GitHub login or per-user ACLs.
+- Candidate version editing does not yet synchronize package lockfiles.
+- GitHub branch rules, PR readiness under a freeze, cancellation recovery, and
+  publication retries need live pilot validation before production use.
+- Analytics collection and historical import helpers are preliminary; the full
+  public popularity and milestones experience is not yet connected.
+
+Do not enable live releases on an existing production project until the pilot
+and recovery paths are validated. Never move a release tag, force-push a source
